title: Textures as a phase-transition probe for quantum spin chains
authors: Heitor P. Casagrande, Isaac M. Carvalho, William J. Munro, Krissia Zawadzki
abstract: The idea of quantum texture has been recently proposed and used as a tool for quantifying coherences and for quantum gate identification. In this work we offer a study on its usage to quantum phase transitions, demonstrating the rugosity metric as a simple tool for effective phase-transition probing. We establish the link between rugosity in the computational basis and the hierarchy of spin correlators, and analyze rugosities defined in the global ground-state and in ground-states belonging to different magnetization sectors (to which we refer to as global vs symmetry-resolved rugosities) to study the phase diagram of the Heisenberg XXZ model. We find distinct rugosity signatures at both transition points. In particular, a sharp feature appears at $Δ=1$ already for small systems, revealing a pronounced sensitivity of the correlation hierarchy encoded by the texture to this point. Since the BKT transition coincides with the isotropic $SU(2)$ point of the XXZ model, this behavior may reflect a particular sensitivity of rugosity to the structure of the spin-correlation hierarchy at isotropy.
summary: This work introduces and applies the rugosity metric, derived from quantum texture, to study quantum phase transitions in the Heisenberg XXZ spin chain. The authors demonstrate that rugosity provides highly sensitive signatures at critical points, particularly highlighting the unique behavior at the BKT transition ($\Delta=1$). This establishes rugosity as a powerful, simple diagnostic tool for probing the structure of quantum correlations across the phase diagram.
main_problem: The paper aims to use the quantum texture, specifically the rugosity metric, as a simple and effective diagnostic tool to probe quantum phase transitions (QPTs) in quantum spin systems.
main_result: Rugosity exhibits distinct, sharp signatures at both the first-order ($\Delta=-1$) and BKT ($\Delta=1$) transition points of the Heisenberg XXZ model, showing sensitivity to the underlying spin-correlation hierarchy.
method: The study employs theoretical analysis, utilizing the rugosity metric derived from quantum texture, and analyzes finite-size scaling behavior across the phase diagram.
model_or_system: The primary system is the Heisenberg XXZ model defined on a spin chain, characterized by the anisotropy parameter $\Delta$. The Hamiltonian is studied in the context of its known QPTs at $\Delta=-1$ and $\Delta=1$.
key_observables: Rugosity ($R$), symmetry-resolved rugosity ($R_Q$), and the extensive coefficient ($\alpha$) derived from finite-size scaling.
important_parameters: The anisotropy parameter $\Delta$, which tunes the system between different magnetic phases, and the system size $N$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that rugosity is a powerful witness for QPTs, and that the finite-size scaling can be accurately modeled by $R(N) = \alpha N +  eta \ln N + c$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of rugosity on $\Delta$ for different magnetization sectors, showing parity effects at $\Delta=-1$ and a peak at $\Delta=1$. Scaling analysis confirms the dominance of the extensive term $\alpha N$ near transitions.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the concept of quantum texture and rugosity, applies it to the XXZ model, analyzes the results by comparing global vs. symmetry-resolved rugosities across the phase diagram, and concludes by interpreting the observed signatures at the critical points.
why_interesting: The use of a geometric/information-theoretic measure (rugosity) to characterize fundamental physical transitions (QPTs) provides a novel, potentially universal diagnostic tool for strongly correlated quantum matter.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Symmetry-resolved rugosity RSz versus ∆for different magnetization sectors. The parity dependence of the symmetry-resolved rugosity sectors can be clearly seen at the point ∆= −1, but the peak at ∆= +1 is present at every sector but the fully polarized ones.

FIG. 2. Global rugosity R versus anisotropy ∆for different system sizes. Lighter tones correspond to smaller sizes, and darker tones to larger sizes. We see a consistent trend among all system-sizes: a slow increase starting at ∆= −1 and a pronounced peak at ∆= 1.

FIG. 3. Finite-size scaling of the rugosity at the phase- transition points ∆= {−1, 1}. Symbols denote numerical data, while solid lines correspond to fits using R(N) = αN + β log N + c. Insets show the ratio |αN|/|γ|, with γ = β log N + c; the red horizontal line marks |αN|/|γ| = 1, where extensive and sub-leading contributions have equal magnitude.
FIG. 4. Extensive coefficient α extracted from fits of the form R(N) = αN +β log N +c as a function of ∆. Vertical dashed lines indicate the transition points at ∆= ±1.
